title: Python power tools
tagline: Read, reason about and fix code
summary: The rest of the Python an AI programmer needs: dictionaries, tuples and sets, functions and scope, comprehensions, zip and generators, how names refer to objects (and the mutation traps examiners love), classes and the fit/predict pattern, and exceptions and systematic debugging.
syllabus: Functions, scope, *args/**kwargs; comprehensions, zip, enumerate, generators
Object references, is vs ==, mutating arguments

lessons.title: Dictionaries, tuples and sets
lessons.summary: Look things up by key, use fixed tuples and unique sets, and know which types are mutable.
objectives: You can create and update dictionaries, including an empty one
You can choose between list, tuple, dict and set for a task
You can classify Python types as mutable or immutable

concepts.name: Dictionaries: key to value
concepts.explain: A dict maps keys to values, for example {'kopi': 1.2, 'teh': 1.1}. Both {} and dict() create an empty dict. Looking up by key is very fast because Python hashes the key to jump straight to its slot, with no scanning.
concepts.analogy: Like a hawker centre's stall numbers: say '#01-23' and you walk straight there without checking every stall.

visual.shows: Keys passing through a hash function into numbered buckets, then a lookup jumping straight to the right bucket.
visual.interaction: Add key/value pairs, look keys up, and try a missing key to trigger a KeyError (compare with .get()).
visual.aha: Dicts trade memory for instant lookup, which is why word counts and caches use them.

concepts.name: Tuples and sets
concepts.explain: A tuple, such as (3, 4), is an ordered sequence you can't change. Tensor shapes and function return pairs are usually tuples. A set keeps only unique items and supports union, intersection and difference.
concepts.analogy: A tuple is your NRIC: fixed once issued. A set is a CCA attendance list: each name appears once.

visual.shows: Two overlapping circles holding the items of set A and set B, with the result of the chosen operation highlighted.
visual.interaction: Edit the two sets and toggle between |, &, - and ^. Add a duplicate item and watch it disappear.
visual.aha: Sets remove duplicates automatically, and set operations are Venn diagrams in code.

concepts.name: Mutable vs immutable
concepts.explain: list, dict and set are mutable: you can change them after creation. int, float, str and tuple are immutable, so any 'change' really creates a new object. This decides whether a function can alter your data and what can be a dict key.
concepts.analogy: A whiteboard (mutable) versus a printed certificate (immutable): you can wipe and rewrite one, but you'd have to reprint the other.

visual.shows: Cards for six types, each with a 'try to change it' button that runs an item assignment.
visual.interaction: Click to attempt the change. A mutable type updates; an immutable type throws a TypeError, which is shown and explained.
visual.aha: Lists and dicts can change under you, while strings and tuples can't.

checkpoint_focus: Which type is mutable (cf. 2026 Prelim Q77)

lessons.title: Functions: reusable recipes
lessons.summary: Define functions with parameters, defaults and return values, and understand scope and *args/**kwargs.
objectives: You can write a function that returns a value
You can predict which variable a name refers to (scope)
You can explain what *args and **kwargs collect

concepts.name: def, parameters and return
concepts.explain: def area(w, h): return w * h packages a calculation under a name. Parameters receive the inputs, and return hands a value back to the caller. print only displays a value and gives back None. Default values, as in def f(x, lr=0.1), make an argument optional.
concepts.analogy: Like a drink-vending machine: put in coins and a choice (arguments), and a can comes out (return value).

visual.shows: A machine box with input slots for each parameter, an output chute, and the function code above it.
visual.interaction: Type argument values and run. Toggle 'return' to 'print' and see that the output chute delivers None.
visual.aha: return passes a value on so later code can use it; print just shows it on screen.

concepts.name: Scope: local vs global
concepts.explain: Variables created inside a function are local: they exist only while it runs. When Python looks up a name, it checks local first, then global. This stops functions from accidentally clobbering each other's variables.
concepts.analogy: Like what's said in a classroom versus the whole-school PA system: a class-only announcement doesn't reach other classes.

visual.shows: Nested bubbles for the global and function frames, each listing its variables, with the current name lookup animated as an arrow.
visual.interaction: Step through code that uses the same name x inside and outside a function. Predict each print before stepping.
visual.aha: The same name can mean different things in different scopes, and lookup goes from the inside out.

concepts.name: *args and **kwargs
concepts.explain: *args collects any number of extra positional arguments into a tuple. **kwargs collects extra keyword arguments into a dict. They let a function accept a flexible number of inputs, a pattern used throughout ML libraries.
concepts.analogy: Like a 'pack all extras here' bag at check-in: any additional items are bundled together.

visual.shows: Arguments flying into a function call and being sorted into named parameters, an args tuple and a kwargs dict.
visual.interaction: Edit the call, for example f(1, 2, 3, lr=0.1, epochs=5), and watch where each argument lands.
visual.aha: *args becomes a tuple and **kwargs becomes a dict. Nothing magic, just packing.

lessons.title: Comprehensions, zip, enumerate and generators
lessons.summary: Write compact loops and produce values lazily.
objectives: You can predict the output of a list comprehension
You can use zip and enumerate correctly
You can explain how a generator saves memory

concepts.name: List comprehensions
concepts.explain: [x**2 for x in range(3)] builds [0, 1, 4] in one line. Read it as 'x squared, for each x in range(3)'. Adding a filter, as in [x for x in nums if x > 0], keeps only some items.
concepts.analogy: Like a juice stall's conveyor: fruits go in, the ones that pass inspection are juiced, and cups come out in order.

visual.shows: Input values riding a conveyor through a filter gate and an expression box, then dropping into an output list.
visual.interaction: Edit the expression and the filter, then play to watch each value either pass or get rejected.
visual.aha: A comprehension is just a for loop with append, written compactly.

concepts.name: zip and enumerate
concepts.explain: zip([1, 2], ['a', 'b']) pairs items up: (1, 'a'), (2, 'b'). It stops at the shorter list and returns an iterator, not a list. enumerate(items) gives (index, item) pairs, so you rarely need range(len(...)).
concepts.analogy: Like a zip on a jacket: teeth from two sides interlock pair by pair.

visual.shows: Two lists of different lengths zipping together into tuples, with the leftover items greyed out.
visual.interaction: Change the list lengths and toggle between zip and enumerate. Wrap the result in list() to see the materialised output.
visual.aha: zip stops at the shortest list, and it gives you an iterator you can only loop through once.

concepts.name: Generators and lazy evaluation
concepts.explain: A generator function uses yield to produce values one at a time, only when asked. It doesn't build the whole list in memory, which is how PyTorch DataLoaders stream huge datasets. Once a generator is used up, it is empty.
concepts.analogy: Like a queue-number machine at a clinic: it prints the next number only when the next patient arrives, not all 500 numbers at once.

visual.shows: A memory bar comparing a list of one million squares with a generator of the same squares, plus a 'next()' button.
visual.interaction: Toggle between list and generator to compare memory, and press next() repeatedly to pull values one by one until StopIteration.
visual.aha: Generators trade 'all at once' for 'on demand', which saves huge amounts of memory.

lessons.title: Names, references and surprises
lessons.summary: Why changing one list can change 'another', is vs ==, and mutable default arguments.
objectives: You can draw names-and-objects diagrams for assignments
You can explain the difference between is and ==
You can predict what happens when a function modifies a list argument
You can explain why a mutable default argument such as items=[] keeps growing across calls

concepts.name: Names point to objects
concepts.explain: After a = [1, 2] and b = a, both names point to the same list, so b.append(3) also changes what a shows. Assignment copies the arrow, not the object. Use a.copy() or list(a) when you need a separate list.
concepts.analogy: Like two people sharing a Google Doc link: if one edits, the other sees the edit, because it is one document.

visual.shows: A Python-Tutor-style diagram with names on the left, objects on the right and arrows between them, updated line by line.
visual.interaction: Step through aliasing, copying and reassignment snippets, predicting each printed result before you reveal it.
visual.aha: Two names, one object. Mutation through either name shows up in both.

concepts.name: is vs ==
concepts.explain: == asks whether two values are equal. is asks whether they are the very same object in memory. Two separate lists [1, 2] are == but not is. Use 'is' mainly for None checks.
concepts.analogy: Twins are equal (==) but are not the same person (is).

visual.shows: Two names with arrows to objects, plus two lamps labelled == and is.
visual.interaction: Toggle between 'same object' and 'equal copy' setups and see which lamp lights. id() values are shown on hover.
visual.aha: Equality compares contents; identity compares arrows.

concepts.name: Functions that mutate their arguments
concepts.explain: Passing a list to a function passes a reference, so if the function appends to it, the caller's list changes. A mutable default like def f(x=[]) is created once and shared across calls, which is a classic bug. Use None as the default and create the list inside.
concepts.analogy: Like lending your notebook to a friend: they write in YOUR notebook, not a copy.

visual.shows: Caller and function frames whose names point to the same list object, with the list growing during the call.
visual.interaction: Run the buggy mutable-default function three times and watch the shared list grow, then apply the None fix and rerun.
visual.aha: Mutable arguments can be changed by the function. This shows up in exam MCQs.

concepts.name: The mutable default argument trap
concepts.explain: Default argument values are created once, when the function is defined. def add(x, items=[]) therefore shares one list across calls, so it keeps growing. The fix is items=None and creating a new list inside.
concepts.analogy: A shared sign-up sheet left at the counter: every customer writes on the same sheet instead of getting a fresh one.

visual.shows: Three calls to the buggy function with the single default list growing in memory, then the fixed version creating a new list each call.
visual.interaction: Step calls; toggle the fix on and off.
visual.aha: Defaults are evaluated once, not every call.

checkpoint_focus: Modifying a list passed to a function (cf. 2026 Prelim Q83)
def f(x, items=[]) shares one list across calls; use items=None

lessons.title: Classes and objects
lessons.summary: Build your own types with attributes and methods, the pattern behind scikit-learn models and PyTorch modules.
objectives: You can define a class with __init__ and methods
You can explain self and instance attributes
You can write a tiny model class with fit and predict
You can read an abstract base class and implement its abstract methods in a subclass

concepts.name: Class = blueprint, object = instance
concepts.explain: A class describes what its objects store (attributes) and can do (methods). __init__ runs when you create an object and sets up its attributes on self. Each object keeps its own copy of the data.
concepts.analogy: Like a BTO flat floor plan (class) and the actual flats built from it (objects): same layout, different families inside.

visual.shows: A class blueprint card stamping out three object cards, each with different attribute values.
visual.interaction: Edit the constructor arguments and stamp new objects, then click an object to inspect its attributes.
visual.aha: One class can make many independent objects.

concepts.name: Methods and the fit/predict pattern
concepts.explain: A method is a function attached to an object that can read and change self. A tiny MeanPredictor class with fit(y), which stores self.mean_, and predict(), which returns it, follows the same pattern as every scikit-learn model. Objects remember what they learned.
concepts.analogy: Like a student who studies (fit) and then answers questions from memory (predict).

visual.shows: The MeanPredictor code beside a live inspector panel of the object's attributes.
visual.interaction: Call predict() before fit() and see the error, then call fit() and watch self.mean_ appear, then predict() again.
visual.aha: fit changes the object's state, and predict uses that state. This is the scikit-learn API.

concepts.name: Inheritance
concepts.explain: class MyNet(nn.Module) creates a child class that inherits all of the parent's methods. You override the ones you need, such as forward, and call super().__init__() so the parent can set itself up. PyTorch models are built exactly this way.
concepts.analogy: Like a new hawker stall inheriting its parent stall's recipes and changing only the chilli.

visual.shows: A parent class box with its methods, and a child box that inherits them, with overridden methods highlighted.
visual.interaction: Click a method on the child to see whether Python finds it on the child or walks up to the parent.
visual.aha: Inheritance lets you reuse a whole framework by writing only the parts that differ.

concepts.name: Abstract base classes
concepts.explain: An abstract base class (ABC) is a template that other classes must complete. With from abc import ABC, abstractmethod, a class Loss(ABC) that declares @abstractmethod def gradient(self, y, y_pred) cannot be created directly, and a subclass that forgets to define gradient raises TypeError when you try to create it. Shared code, such as a predict loop, lives once in the base class and each child fills in only the parts that differ. The 2026 Final's gradient-boosting scaffold (BaseGradientBoosting with L1 and L2 variants) uses exactly this pattern.
concepts.analogy: A form with some boxes pre-printed and others marked 'must fill in': every copy shares the printed parts, and an incomplete form is rejected at the counter.

visual.shows: A base-class card with concrete methods (solid) and abstract methods (dashed slots), and two child-class cards (L1Loss and L2Loss) that plug code into the dashed slots; a console shows what happens when you create each class.
visual.interaction: Try to create the base class (TypeError), then a child with a missing method (TypeError), then a complete child (works); click a method call to see whether base or child code runs.
visual.aha: Abstract methods are the blanks you must fill, so reading which methods are abstract tells you exactly what an exam scaffold expects you to write.

checkpoint_focus: Reading class code and predicting attribute values
ABC and @abstractmethod: what must be filled in

lessons.title: Exceptions and debugging
lessons.summary: Know the common exceptions, handle errors with try/except, and debug systematically.
objectives: You can name the cause of IndexError, KeyError, TypeError, ValueError and ZeroDivisionError
You can write correct try/except/finally blocks
You can apply a step-by-step debugging routine

concepts.name: Common exceptions
concepts.explain: IndexError means a position is out of range, KeyError means a dict key is missing, and TypeError means the wrong type for an operation. ValueError means the right type but a bad value, as in int('abc'). ZeroDivisionError is dividing by zero. Knowing the cause from the name saves minutes in an exam.
concepts.analogy: Like the warning lights on a car dashboard: each symbol points to a different problem.

visual.shows: A grid of one-line buggy snippets, each with a hidden exception type.
visual.interaction: Guess each snippet's exception, run it to check, and then reveal the one-line fix.
visual.aha: Each exception type points to a specific family of causes.

concepts.name: try / except / finally
concepts.explain: Code in try runs normally. If an exception occurs, Python jumps to the matching except block. finally always runs, error or not, so it suits clean-up. Catch specific exceptions, because a bare except can hide real bugs.
concepts.analogy: Like a wet-weather plan for sports day: try the field, fall back to the hall if it rains, and pack up the chairs either way.

visual.shows: A flowchart of the try, except, else and finally paths, with the code beside it.
visual.interaction: Toggle an input that does or doesn't cause an error, then play to see which path runs and which prints appear.
visual.aha: finally always runs, and the except block only runs if a matching error happens.

concepts.name: Systematic debugging
concepts.explain: Debug in a routine: reproduce the bug, read the error, and print or assert intermediate values. Then narrow down the location by halving the code you suspect. Off-by-one errors and wrong variable names are the most common culprits.
concepts.analogy: Like a doctor's diagnosis: check the symptoms, run tests, and narrow down the cause before treating.

visual.shows: A buggy average() function that returns the wrong value, with clickable lines.
visual.interaction: Click lines to insert print probes and see a trace of the values, then click the line you think is wrong to reveal the off-by-one bug.
visual.aha: Printing intermediate values turns a mystery into a visible wrong number.

checkpoint_focus: Likely cause of IndexError (cf. 2026 Prelim Q126)
